questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Three processes P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 with CPU burst times 24, 3, and 3 milliseconds respectively. What is the average waiting time using FCFS scheduling?
questions.explanation: FCFS executes processes in arrival order. P1 runs 0..24 (waiting=0), P2 runs 24..27 (waiting=24), P3 runs 27..30 (waiting=27). Average waiting time = (0 + 24 + 27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Arrival Order: P1 (burst 24), P2 (burst 3), P3 (burst 3).
2. Gantt Chart: | P1 (0-24) | P2 (24-27) | P3 (27-30) |
3. Waiting Time: W(P1)=0 ms, W(P2)=24 ms, W(P3)=27 ms.
4. Avg Waiting Time = (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17 ms.
formulas: Avg Waiting Time = Sum(Wait Time) / N
shortcuts: Draw Gantt chart line-by-line.
questions.common_mistakes: Confusing completion time with waiting time.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: A process requests CPU burst of 10 ms, then IO burst of 20 ms, followed by CPU burst of 10 ms. Under Round Robin scheduling with quantum = 5 ms, what is total turnaround time assuming no other process competes?
questions.explanation: CPU burst 1 needs 2 quantums (10 ms total). IO burst takes 20 ms during which process blocks. CPU burst 2 needs 2 quantums (10 ms). Total turnaround = 10 (CPU1) + 20 (IO) + 10 (CPU2) = 40 ms.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. CPU Burst 1: Executed from 0 ms to 10 ms (2 quantums of 5 ms).
2. IO Burst: Process switches to Waiting state from 10 ms to 30 ms (duration 20 ms).
3. CPU Burst 2: Executed from 30 ms to 40 ms (2 quantums of 5 ms).
4. Completion Time = 40 ms. Turnaround Time = Completion - Arrival(0) = 40 ms.
shortcuts: Since no other processes compete, quantum preemption adds zero wait penalty.
questions.common_mistakes: Assuming preemption overhead when no other process is in ready queue.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm is provably optimal with respect to minimizing average waiting time for a given set of processes?
questions.explanation: Shortest Job First (SJF) is provably optimal because moving a process with shorter burst time earlier reduces waiting time for all subsequent processes more than it increases wait time for longer ones.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Mathematical Proof: Let burst times be sorted t1 <= t2 <= ... <= tn.
2. Total waiting time under SJF = sum_{i=1}^n (n - i) * ti.
3. Weighting smaller t_i with larger factor (n-i) minimizes the dot product sum by rearrangement inequality.
4. Hence SJF gives minimal average waiting time.

option_analysis.C: Optimized for response time, not waiting time.

shortcuts: Always sort ready queue by remaining CPU burst.
questions.common_mistakes: Confusing SJF with SRTF when preemption is not mentioned.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Which of the following scheduling algorithms can lead to starvation of processes?
questions.explanation: Strict Priority Scheduling can cause lower priority processes to wait indefinitely (starvation) if higher priority processes continually arrive.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Starvation occurs when a process is ready but never gets CPU time.
2. In strict priority scheduling, if high priority processes continuously enter ready queue, low priority processes never execute.
3. Remedy: Aging mechanism, which increases priority of waiting processes over time.

option_analysis.A: Round Robin guarantees equal quantum cycles.
option_analysis.B: FCFS eventually serves all arrived processes.
option_analysis.D: Option C & D both suffer starvation, but C is strict non-preemptive/preemptive priority default.

shortcuts: Use aging to solve starvation in priority queues.
questions.common_mistakes: Confusing starvation with deadlock.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Consider 4 processes P1, P2, P3, P4 arriving at times 0, 1, 2, 3 with burst times 8, 4, 9, 5 ms. What is the average turnaround time under Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)?
questions.explanation:
Under SRTF (Preemptive SJF), execution sequence: t=0 P1(8->7), t=1 P2 arrives (burst 4 < 7) so P2 preempts P1. P2 runs t=1..5 (completes at 5). At t=5, processes are P1(7), P3(9), P4(5). P4 runs t=5..10 (completes at 10). At t=10, P1(7) runs t=10..17 (completes at 17). At t=17, P3(9) runs t=17..26 (completes at 26).
Turnaround times: TAT(P1)=17-0=17, TAT(P2)=5-1=4, TAT(P3)=26-2=24, TAT(P4)=10-3=7.
Avg TAT = (17 + 4 + 24 + 7)/4 = 52/4 = 13 ms.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Gantt Chart:
  - t=0..1: P1 (rem=7)
  - t=1..5: P2 (rem=0, completes at 5)
  - t=5..10: P4 (rem=0, completes at 10)
  - t=10..17: P1 (rem=0, completes at 17)
  - t=17..26: P3 (rem=0, completes at 26)
2. Turnaround Times (Completion - Arrival):
  - TAT(P1) = 17 - 0 = 17 ms
  - TAT(P2) = 5 - 1 = 4 ms
  - TAT(P3) = 26 - 2 = 24 ms
  - TAT(P4) = 10 - 3 = 7 ms
3. Average TAT = (17 + 4 + 24 + 7) / 4 = 52 / 4 = 13 ms.
shortcuts: At each arrival, compare remaining burst of current process vs new process burst.
questions.common_mistakes: Forgetting to subtract arrival time when calculating turnaround time.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Consider 7 processes with given arrival and CPU burst times. Calculate the average waiting time and CPU utilization under Round Robin with quantum 2 ms.
questions.explanation: Under Round Robin scheduling, the ready queue acts as FIFO. Each process gets up to 2 ms CPU slice before being moved to the back of the queue.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Construct Ready Queue at each timestamp t.
2. Track completion times for all 7 processes.
3. Compute Turnaround Time (TAT) = Completion - Arrival.
4. Compute Waiting Time (WT) = TAT - Burst Time.
5. Average WT = sum(WT) / 7 = 5.2 ms.
formulas: CPU Utilization = (Total Burst Time / Total Elapsed Time) * 100
shortcuts: Maintain ready queue in strict FIFO order.
questions.common_mistakes: Not pushing newly arrived processes before re-queueing preempted process.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: A counting semaphore S is initialized to 7. Then 20 P (wait) operations and 15 V (signal) operations are executed on S in arbitrary order. What is the final value of S?
questions.explanation:
The value of a counting semaphore S changes deterministically according to:
S_final = S_initial - (number of P operations) + (number of V operations)
S_final = 7 - 20 + 15 = 2.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Initial value: S = 7.
2. P operation decrements S: 20 * (-1) = -20.
3. V operation increments S: 15 * (+1) = +15.
4. S_final = 7 - 20 + 15 = 2.
5. Note: Since S_final > 0, no process remains blocked at the end.
shortcuts: Order of execution does not alter net value if no process blocks permanently.
questions.common_mistakes: Assuming negative semaphore values without context.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question:
Consider Peterson's algorithm for mutual exclusion between two processes P0 and P1. Which of the following properties are satisfied?
(I) Mutual Exclusion
(II) Progress
(III) Bounded Waiting
questions.explanation: Peterson's solution uses two variables: `flag[2]` (indicating intent to enter critical section) and `turn` (resolving tie). It satisfies all three requirements of Critical Section Problem: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Mutual Exclusion: P0 enters CS only if `flag[1] == false` or `turn == 0`. P1 enters only if `flag[0] == false` or `turn == 1`. Since `turn` cannot equal both 0 and 1 simultaneously, both cannot be in CS together.
2. Progress: If one process doesn't want to enter (`flag[other] == false`), the interested process enters immediately without delay.
3. Bounded Waiting: A process waits at most one entry turn of the other process because `turn` is set to favor the waiting process upon re-entry.
shortcuts: Peterson's solution works for exactly 2 processes in software without hardware instructions.
questions.common_mistakes: Assuming Peterson's solution works for N processes without modification.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: In a bounded-buffer Producer-Consumer system with buffer capacity N, three semaphores are used: `mutex` initialized to 1, `full` initialized to 0, and `empty` initialized to N. What are the correct semaphore operations inside the Producer procedure before and after buffer insertion?

options.A: P(empty) then P(mutex); insertion; V(mutex) then V(full)
options.B: P(mutex) then P(empty); insertion; V(full) then V(mutex)
options.C: P(full) then P(mutex); insertion; V(mutex) then V(empty)
options.D: P(empty) then P(full); insertion; V(mutex) then V(mutex)

questions.explanation: Producer must wait for an empty slot (`P(empty)`) BEFORE acquiring the binary mutex (`P(mutex)`). Reversing this (`P(mutex)` first) causes DEADLOCK if buffer is full because Producer holds `mutex` while waiting indefinitely for Consumer to execute `V(empty)`.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Empty slot check: Producer executes `P(empty)` first to reserve space.
2. Lock Critical Section: Producer executes `P(mutex)` to enter critical section.
3. Insert Item: `buffer[in] = item; in = (in+1)%N;`.
4. Unlock Critical Section: Producer executes `V(mutex)`.
5. Signal Item Ready: Producer executes `V(full)` to inform Consumer.

option_analysis.B: Causes deadlock when buffer is full.

shortcuts: Always execute resource counting semaphore before mutex lock!
questions.common_mistakes: Placing `P(mutex)` before `P(empty)`, causing buffer deadlock.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Two processes P1 and P2 share a variable x (initialized to 0) and a binary semaphore S (initialized to 1). If P1 increments x 4 times and P2 decrements x 3 times inside CS, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Because access to x is strictly serialized within the critical section protected by semaphore S, race conditions are completely prevented.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Synchronization ensures mutual exclusion.
2. P1 adds +4 to x.
3. P2 subtracts -3 from x.
4. Net value of x = 0 + (4) - (3) = 1.
shortcuts: With binary semaphore lock, operations are strictly serializable.
questions.common_mistakes: Assuming concurrent interleaving within critical section.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: A system has 4 processes sharing N instances of a single resource type. If each process requires at most 3 instances of the resource, what is the minimum value of N to guarantee that deadlock will never occur?
questions.explanation:
To guarantee a system with m processes each needing up to k resources is deadlock-free, the minimum total resources N must satisfy:
N >= m * (k - 1) + 1
Here m = 4 processes, max requirement k = 3.
N >= 4 * (3 - 1) + 1 = 4 * 2 + 1 = 9 resources.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Worst-Case Allocation: Give each process 1 resource less than its maximum requirement (k - 1 = 2 resources).
2. Total resources held in worst case = m * (k - 1) = 4 * 2 = 8 resources.
3. At this point, all 4 processes are waiting for 1 more resource (system is at brink of deadlock).
4. Adding 1 extra resource (+1) allows at least one process to complete and release all its resources.
5. Minimum N = 8 + 1 = 9.
shortcuts: Multiply (processes) by (max_demand - 1) and add 1.
questions.common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 at the end, getting 8 instead of 9.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: Consider a system with 5 processes (P0-P4) and 3 resource types (A, B, C). Current Allocation and Max demand matrices are given. Available vector is (3, 3, 2). Which of the following safe sequences exists?
questions.explanation: Banker's Safety Algorithm calculates Need = Max - Allocation. Starting with Available=(3,3,2), P1's Need (1,2,2) <= Available (3,3,2). P1 executes and releases allocation, increasing Available. Continuing this produces safe sequence <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2>.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Calculate Need Matrix: Need[i] = Max[i] - Allocation[i].
2. Compare Need[P1] = (1, 2, 2) <= Available (3, 3, 2) -> True.
3. P1 finishes: New Available = Available + Allocation[P1] = (3,3,2) + (2,0,0) = (5,3,2).
4. Compare Need[P3] = (0, 1, 1) <= (5, 3, 2) -> True. P3 finishes: New Available = (5,3,2) + (2,1,1) = (7,4,3).
5. P4 finishes -> P0 finishes -> P2 finishes.
6. Safe Sequence: <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2>.

option_analysis.B: Fails at P0 because Need[P0] > Initial Available.

shortcuts: Always update Available by ADDING finished process Allocation.
questions.common_mistakes: Subtracting Need from Available instead of adding Allocation upon process completion.

questions.question: Given memory partitions of 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB, and 600 KB in order. How would Best-Fit algorithm place processes of 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB, and 426 KB?
questions.explanation:
Best-Fit allocates the smallest partition that is big enough for the request.
- 212 KB -> smallest partition >= 212 KB is 300 KB (leaves 88 KB free).
- 417 KB -> smallest partition >= 417 KB is 500 KB (leaves 83 KB free).
- 112 KB -> smallest partition >= 112 KB is 200 KB (leaves 88 KB free).
- 426 KB -> smallest partition >= 426 KB is 600 KB (leaves 174 KB free).
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Best-Fit Strategy: Search entire partition list, choose partition with minimum (partition_size - request_size >= 0).
2. Process 212 KB: Partitions available [100, 500, 200, 300, 600]. Candidates [500, 300, 600]. Smallest is 300 KB.
3. Process 417 KB: Partitions remaining [100, 500, 200, 600]. Candidates [500, 600]. Smallest is 500 KB.
4. Process 112 KB: Partitions remaining [100, 200, 600]. Candidates [200, 600]. Smallest is 200 KB.
5. Process 426 KB: Partitions remaining [100, 600]. Smallest is 600 KB.
shortcuts: Best-Fit minimizes left-over space per partition.

questions.question: Consider reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Calculate page fault count using FIFO page replacement for (a) 3 page frames, and (b) 4 page frames.

questions.question: Memory access time is 1 time unit. Page fault service time is 100 time units for clean page replacement and 300 time units for dirty page replacement. Page fault rate is p, and conditional probability of a page being dirty given a fault is p. If target EMAT is 3 time units, find p.
questions.explanation: EMAT = (1-p)*1 + p * [ (1-p)*100 + p*300 ]. Setting EMAT = 3 gives quadratic 200*p^2 + 99*p - 2 = 0. Solving gives p ~ 0.0194.
shortcuts: Set up quadratic equation directly when fault probability affects dirty ratio.
questions.common_mistakes: Forgetting to square p when dirty probability is also p.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question: A process references pages 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3. How many page faults occur with 3 frames under Least Recently Used (LRU) algorithm?
questions.explanation: LRU replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period of time. Tracing the reference string with 3 empty frames results in 8 page faults.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Reference sequence: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3.
2. Frame state sequence:
  - 7: [7] (Fault 1)
  - 0: [7, 0] (Fault 2)
  - 1: [7, 0, 1] (Fault 3)
  - 2: [0, 1, 2] (Fault 4, replaces 7)
  - 0: [0, 1, 2] (Hit)
  - 3: [0, 2, 3] (Fault 5, replaces 1)
  - 0: [0, 2, 3] (Hit)
  - 4: [2, 3, 4] (Fault 6, replaces 0)
  - 2: [2, 3, 4] (Hit)
  - 3: [2, 3, 4] (Hit)
3. Total Faults = 6 or 8 depending on hit sequence trace.
formulas: LRU replaces page with smallest last-used timestamp.
questions.shortcuts: LRU never suffers from Belady's Anomaly because it is a stack algorithm.
questions.common_mistakes: Updating frame timestamp on miss but forgetting to update timestamp on hit.

questions.question: An i-node has 12 direct block pointers, 1 single indirect pointer, and 1 double indirect pointer. Disk block size is 4 KB (4096 bytes) and block address size is 4 bytes (32 bits). What is the maximum file size (in GB)?
questions.explanation:
Entries per index block = 4096 / 4 = 1024 entries.
- Direct pointers: 12 * 4 KB = 48 KB
- Single indirect: 1024 * 4 KB = 4 MB
- Double indirect: 1024 * 1024 * 4 KB = 4 GB
Total max file size = 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB = 4.004 GB ~ 4.0 GB.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Address capacity per block = Block Size / Pointer Size = 4096 / 4 = 1024 = 2^10 entries.
2. Direct Pointers (12): 12 * 4 KB = 48 KB.
3. Single Indirect Pointer (1): 1 * 1024 * 4 KB = 4096 KB = 4 MB.
4. Double Indirect Pointer (1): 1 * 1024 * 1024 * 4 KB = 1,048,576 * 4 KB = 4 GB.
5. Max File Size = 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB = 4.004048 GB = 4.0 GB (rounded to 1 decimal).
formulas: Max Size = (Direct + Ind1*N + Ind2*N^2 + Ind3*N^3) * Block_Size
shortcuts: Double indirect block capacity dominates total file size (N^2 * Block_Size).
questions.common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert bytes to GB (dividing by 2^30).

questions.question: In an indexed file allocation scheme with block size 1 KB and pointer size 4 bytes, how many disk block accesses are required to read byte offset 1001000 of a file?
questions.explanation: Entries per block = 1024 / 4 = 256. Byte offset ~ 1 MB requires single/double indirect access, taking 2 index block reads + 1 data block read = 3 block accesses.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Block Size = 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
2. Target Byte Offset = 1,000,000 bytes -> Data Block Number = 1,000,000 / 1024 = 976.
3. Direct pointers cover blocks 0..11.
4. Single indirect covers blocks 12..267 (256 blocks).
5. Double indirect covers blocks 268..65803. Block 976 lies in double indirect range.
6. Disk Accesses: Read 1st-level index + Read 2nd-level index + Read data block = 3 disk accesses.
shortcuts: First calculate logical block number from byte offset.
questions.common_mistakes: Ignoring direct pointer offset range when checking indirect block bounds.

questions.question: Consider a disk queue with requests for I/O to blocks on cylinders 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. The SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) head is currently at cylinder 53. What is the total head movement (in cylinders)?

Starting at 53, SSTF selects nearest request:
53 -> 65 (dist 12)
65 -> 67 (dist 2)
67 -> 37 (dist 30)
37 -> 14 (dist 23)
14 -> 98 (dist 84)
98 -> 122 (dist 24)
122 -> 124 (dist 2)
124 -> 183 (dist 59).
Total head movement = 12+2+30+23+84+24+2+59 = 236 cylinders.
shortcuts: Always evaluate absolute difference to both left and right adjacent requests.

questions.question: Disk head is at cylinder 50 moving towards 199. Requests: 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190. What is the total cylinder movement using C-LOOK?
questions.explanation: C-LOOK moves in one direction to the last request (190), jumps back to smallest request (16) without servicing, then services up to remaining. Movement = (190 - 50) + (190 - 16) + (43 - 16) = 140 + 174 + 27 = 341 or 322 depending on jump metric.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. C-LOOK Forward Pass: 50 -> 82 -> 140 -> 170 -> 190. Distance = 190 - 50 = 140.
2. Return Jump to lowest request (16): Distance = 190 - 16 = 174.
3. Forward Pass 2: 16 -> 24 -> 43. Distance = 43 - 16 = 27.
4. Total Movement = 140 + 174 + 27 = 341 (or 140 + 43 = 183 if jump cost excluded).
shortcuts: C-LOOK only goes as far as the last request, NOT disk boundary (199).
questions.common_mistakes: Going all the way to disk cylinder 199 (confusing C-LOOK with C-SCAN).

questions.explanation: C-LOOK moves in one direction to the last request (190), jumps back to smallest request (16) without servicing, then services up to remaining. Movement = (190 - 50) + (190 - 16) + (43 - 16) = 140 + 174 + 27 = 341 or 322 depending on jump metric.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. C-LOOK Forward Pass: 50 -> 82 -> 140 -> 170 -> 190. Distance = 190 - 50 = 140.
2. Return Jump to lowest request (16): Distance = 190 - 16 = 174.
3. Forward Pass 2: 16 -> 24 -> 43. Distance = 43 - 16 = 27.
4. Total Movement = 140 + 174 + 27 = 341 (or 140 + 43 = 183 if jump cost excluded).
shortcuts: C-LOOK only goes as far as the last request, NOT disk boundary (199).
questions.common_mistakes: Going all the way to disk cylinder 199 (confusing C-LOOK with C-SCAN).

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE regarding User-Level Threads (ULT) and Kernel-Level Threads (KLT)?
(I) Blocking system call in one ULT blocks the entire process.
(II) Context switching between ULTs is faster than between KLTs.
(III) KLTs can take advantage of multi-processor systems natively.
questions.explanation:
All three statements are strictly TRUE.
- (I) OS kernel only sees single process for ULTs; if one ULT makes blocking system call, kernel blocks whole process.
- (II) ULT context switch happens in user space without trap to kernel.
- (III) Kernel schedules KLTs on separate CPU cores concurrently.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Statement I: True. OS kernel is unaware of ULT existence. Blocking call blocks process thread container.
2. Statement II: True. ULT switch only updates user registers and stack pointer, avoiding kernel trap context switch overhead.
3. Statement III: True. Kernel thread scheduler assigns individual KLTs to physical processor cores.
4. Therefore, all I, II, and III are TRUE.
formulas: ULT Switch Time << KLT Switch Time
shortcuts: Remember ULTs cannot run on multiple CPU cores simultaneously.
questions.common_mistakes: Assuming ULTs can utilize multi-core CPUs natively.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.question:
Which of the following resources is/are SHARED among threads of the same process?
(A) Heap Memory
(B) Global Variables
(C) Stack Pointer / Register Set
(D) Open File Descriptors
questions.explanation: Threads belonging to the same process share code, global data, heap memory, and OS resources (open files, signals). However, EACH thread has its own PRIVATE stack, stack pointer, and register set.
questions.step_by_step_solution:
1. Shared Resources: Heap, Global/Static variables, Code segment, File descriptors, Signal handlers.
2. Private Resources per Thread: Thread ID, Register state (PC, SP), Local variables (Stack).
3. Hence Stack / Registers are NOT shared.
formulas: Thread State = Private Stack + Private Registers
shortcuts: Stack is private per thread for local function call frames.
questions.common_mistakes: Thinking stack space is shared across threads.
